name: Central Processing Unit
summary: A processor that executes instructions and coordinates computation.
description: A CPU repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Registers hold values close to the execution units, while caches reduce the average time required to access memory.
facts: An instruction set defines operations visible to software.
A CPU can contain multiple processing cores.
Registers are smaller and faster than main memory.

name: Machine Instruction
summary: An encoded operation defined by a processor instruction set.
description: A machine instruction identifies an operation and any required operands. Its encoding and behavior belong to an instruction-set architecture rather than to a particular source language.
facts: Instructions can operate on registers, memory addresses or immediate values.
A compiler can translate higher-level operations into machine instructions.

name: Processor Register
summary: A small storage location directly available to processor instructions.
description: Registers hold operands, addresses and control state during instruction execution. Their exact number and roles depend on the instruction-set architecture.
facts: General-purpose registers can hold data or addresses.
A program counter identifies the next instruction position.

name: Processor Cache
summary: A small fast memory that retains recently or nearby accessed data.
description: A processor cache stores copies of memory regions in cache lines. Locality makes those copies useful because programs often revisit data or access neighboring addresses.
facts: A cache hit avoids a slower access to the next memory level.
Cache coherence coordinates copies shared by multiple processors or cores.

name: Main Memory
summary: Addressable storage used for the active data and code of running programs.
description: Main memory provides byte-addressable regions to processors. An operating system maps process-visible virtual addresses onto physical memory and other backing storage.
facts: Main memory is normally volatile.
Memory addresses identify locations rather than the semantic type of their contents.

name: Virtual Memory
summary: An address-space abstraction that separates process addresses from physical storage.
description: Virtual memory lets each process use a logical address space. Page mappings associate ranges of virtual addresses with physical memory, files or reserved regions.
facts: Different processes can map the same virtual address to different physical locations.
Permissions can be applied to individual mapped pages.

name: Memory Page
summary: A fixed-size unit used to map and protect virtual memory.
description: A page table records how virtual pages correspond to physical frames or other backing. Access permissions commonly distinguish reading, writing and instruction execution.
facts: A page fault occurs when an access cannot be completed from the current mapping state.
Page sizes are architecture and operating-system choices.

name: Process
summary: An operating-system abstraction for a running program and its resources.
description: A process combines an address space, execution state and access to operating-system resources. One process can contain multiple threads that share its memory and open resources.
facts: A process identifier distinguishes active processes.
Processes normally have separate virtual address spaces.

name: Thread
summary: A schedulable sequence of execution within a process.
description: Threads in the same process can share memory and resources while retaining their own execution state, including a stack and register context.
facts: A scheduler can pause one thread and resume another.
Shared memory makes synchronization necessary when threads update common state.

name: Scheduler
summary: An operating-system component that chooses which runnable work executes.
description: A scheduler assigns processor time to runnable threads according to policy, priority and available processors. A context switch preserves one execution state and restores another.
facts: Scheduling policy can trade throughput, latency and fairness.
A blocked thread is not runnable until its wait condition changes.

name: System Call
summary: A controlled request from a program to an operating-system service.
description: A system call crosses a protected interface so a process can request operations such as file access, memory mapping or communication.
facts: System-call interfaces validate arguments before using protected resources.
A library function may wrap one or more system calls.

name: Filesystem
summary: A storage organization that names and manages persistent byte sequences.
description: A filesystem maps path components to stored objects and metadata. Directories organize names, while internal records such as inodes can describe object ownership, size and storage locations.
facts: A pathname is resolved component by component.
Filesystem metadata is distinct from file content.

name: Directory
summary: A filesystem object that associates names with other filesystem objects.
description: Directories create a navigable namespace by mapping path components to object references. A directory entry is not the file content itself.
facts: A directory can contain references to files and other directories.
Renaming an entry can change a path without rewriting file content.

name: Inode
summary: A Unix-style filesystem record describing an object and its stored data.
description: An inode stores metadata and references to data blocks, while directory entries associate human-readable names with inode numbers.
facts: A single inode can be referenced by more than one directory entry.
The filename is normally stored in a directory entry rather than in the inode.

name: Network Packet
summary: A bounded unit of data carried through a packet-switched network.
description: A packet combines protocol headers with payload data. Different protocol layers add information needed for addressing, delivery, ordering or application semantics.
facts: Packet headers are interpreted according to their protocol.
A large application message can be carried across multiple packets.

name: Internet Protocol
summary: A network-layer protocol for addressing and forwarding datagrams.
description: IP provides best-effort delivery between addressed interfaces across interconnected networks. Reliability and ordered byte delivery, when required, are provided by higher layers.
facts: An IP address identifies a network interface in a routing context.
IP does not guarantee that every datagram arrives.

name: Transmission Control Protocol
summary: A transport protocol that provides a reliable ordered byte stream.
description: TCP establishes a connection between endpoints, numbers transmitted bytes and retransmits data when necessary. Applications see an ordered stream rather than message boundaries.
facts: TCP uses sequence numbers and acknowledgments.
Flow control protects a receiver from excessive buffered data.

name: Hypertext Transfer Protocol
summary: An application protocol based on requests, responses and resource representations.
description: HTTP defines methods, status codes, fields and message semantics for interacting with resources. Its semantics are independent of a particular representation format.
facts: A client sends a request and a server returns a response.
Status codes classify the outcome of a request.
